title: Twenty items: which sort is cheaper?
hook: Two step-count formulas, one short list. Pick the cheaper sort.

knows: n² grows faster than n log n (quadratic-wall)
doesNotKnow: that constant factors decide which method is cheaper for small inputs, so there is a crossover size below which the slower-growing method loses

misconception: A method with a better growth rate is faster for every input size.
objective: The learner can explain that with costs 8·n² and 64·n·log₂n insertion sort is cheaper up to n = 43 because merge sort's constant 64 outweighs its slower growth at small n, and merge sort wins from n = 44 on.

claims.text: With costs 8·n² (insertion sort) and 64·n·log₂n (merge sort, rounded to whole steps), n = 20 gives 3,200 and 5,532 steps, n = 43 gives 14,792 and 14,933, n = 44 gives 15,488 and 15,374, and n = 100 gives 80,000 and 42,521.
claims.source: insertion() and merge() in src/demos/cs/small-n-favours-the-slow-curve/model.ts; re-run in node by the builder 2026-10-14: 20 -> 3200 / 5532; 43 -> 14792 / 14933; 44 -> 15488 / 15374; 100 -> 80000 / 42521.

claims.text: Under this model insertion sort is cheaper for every n from 2 to 43 and merge sort for every n from 44 to 1,000.
claims.source: Builder's node loop n = 2..1,000 on 2026-10-14: insertion cheaper for 42 consecutive sizes (2-43), merge cheaper for the remaining 957 (44-1,000). The cost formulas are CLRS 3e exercise 1.2-2 (whose answer is n <= 43).

claims.text: The 64 in front of merge sort's cost outweighs its slower growth while n is small; growth rate tells you who wins eventually, not who wins at your size.
claims.source: From c1 and c2: 8n² < 64 n log₂ n exactly when n < 8 log₂ n, which holds for n <= 43 and fails for n >= 44; for large n the n² term dominates any constant.

claims.text: Fast merge sorts hand short pieces to insertion sort.
claims.source: CLRS 3e Problem 2-1 ('Insertion sort on small arrays in merge sort': coarsening the leaves of the recursion). Practical hybrids (e.g. Timsort sorting short runs by binary insertion) do the same. Attribution: fact-checker confirms the problem number from the book; if 'fast merge sorts' cannot be supported, cut to 'merge sort can be sped up by handing short pieces to insertion sort'.

claims.text: The step counts come from a cost model with chosen constants, not timings of real code.
claims.source: Stage caption. The constants 8 and 64 are those of CLRS 3e exercise 1.2-2; the lesson claims nothing about any machine.

recall.question: Method P costs 2·n² steps and method Q costs 50·n steps. Which is cheaper for 10 items?
recall.why: At n = 10, P costs 200 and Q costs 500: Q's constant 50 outweighs its slower growth until n passes 25. Growth rate decides the winner only for large inputs.
